challenges.name: throughput-error-rate-quiz
challenges.title: Read the numbers behind "50 req/s, 2% errors"
challenges.description: Two summaries of the same steady-state window of a POST /submissions load test on CodeDev staging. Decide whether each statement about the numbers is true or false.

questions.question:
Steady-state window 300 s - 900 s of the run (600 s), counted from the result records by end_ms. Latency is measured from intended_ms; the SLO is 800 ms.

completed records ............ 30,000
successful (200-399) ......... 29,400
successful within 800 ms ..... 24,000
errors (status 0 or >= 400) .. 600

Statement: "In this window the API completed 50 requests per second, but only 40 per second were useful to learners under the SLO; the other 10 per second either failed or were too slow."
questions.explanation: True. Throughput = 30,000 / 600 s = 50/s. Goodput counts only successful responses within the latency SLO: 24,000 / 600 s = 40/s. The 10/s difference is 600 errors (1/s) plus 5,400 successes that took longer than 800 ms (9/s). A slow 200 still counts in throughput and does not count as an error, which is why throughput and error rate together can look healthy while learners wait. The misconception is that a 2% error rate means 98% of learners were served well; goodput answers that question directly.

questions.question:
The same window, as the old dashboard computed it:

error_rate = count(status >= 400) / count(all records)

status 200/201 ... 29,400
status 503 ....... 120
status 0 ......... 480   (client timeout after 3 s or connection reset)

Dashboard: "error rate 0.4%"

Statement: "0.4% is the error rate of POST /submissions in this window, because a status 0 has no HTTP status code and so is not an HTTP error."
questions.explanation: False. The dashboard counted 120 / 30,000 = 0.4%, but 480 requests got no answer at all: they timed out or lost the connection. For the learner that is a failed submission, usually the worst kind, so the real error rate is (120 + 480) / 30,000 = 2.0%, five times higher. Timeouts also tend to grow first when a system saturates, so dropping them hides exactly the trend you are testing for. k6's http_req_failed likewise counts a request that got no response as failed. The misconception is that only an HTTP status of 400 or more is an error; success must be defined positively (200-399) and everything else counted as an error.

challenges.name: windowed-throughput-error-goodput
challenges.title: Throughput, error rate and goodput per window
challenges.description:
The load test report for POST /submissions on CodeDev staging said "50 req/s, 0.4% errors". Nobody could say over which interval, whether timeouts were counted, or how many requests were fast enough to matter. Compute the numbers from the raw result records.

Record: {"id", "intended_ms", "start_ms", "end_ms", "status"}, integer ms from test start; status 0 = timeout or connection error; success = 200 <= status < 400, every other status (0 included) is an error; latency for the SLO = end_ms - intended_ms (from the intended send time, lesson 3). Records arrive in any order.

Write summarize(records, window_ms, slo_ms, steady_from_ms, steady_to_ms) in throughput.py:
- A record completes at end_ms, whatever its status. Window k is [k * window_ms, (k + 1) * window_ms): a record ending exactly on a boundary belongs to the window that starts there.
- "windows": one entry per window from k = 0 up to the window of the largest end_ms, empty windows included ([] when there are no records): {"start_ms", "completed", "throughput_rps" (completed / window seconds), "error_pct" (100 * errors / completed, null when completed is 0), "goodput_rps" (successes with latency <= slo_ms / window seconds)}.
- "steady": the same numbers over [steady_from_ms, steady_to_ms) selected by end_ms, as {"completed", "offered_rps" (records whose intended_ms is in the interval / interval seconds), "throughput_rps", "error_pct", "timeouts" (status 0 records completed in the interval), "goodput_rps"}.
- Round every float to 2 decimals (no test value is exactly halfway).
- Validate: window_ms <= 0 -> ValueError("window_ms must be > 0"); steady_to_ms <= steady_from_ms -> ValueError("steady interval is empty").

Input (stdin): {"records": [...], "window_ms": int, "slo_ms": int, "steady": {"from_ms": int, "to_ms": int}}. The runner prints {"windows": [...], "steady": {...}} or {"error": message}.
hints: A request that timed out after 3 s: did it complete, and is it a success? A request that was meant to leave at 100 ms, actually left at 650 ms and was answered at 700 ms: how long did the learner wait?

Check four places: the field you bucket by (end_ms, with window k = end_ms // window_ms), the error test (anything outside 200-399, status 0 included), the latency you compare with the SLO (from intended_ms, not start_ms), and what a window with no records reports (completed 0 and an error_pct of null, not 0).

A similar case: window_ms 2000, slo_ms 300, records ending at 2500 ms (200, intended 2100), 3000 ms (status 0) and 3990 ms (200, intended 3500). Window 0 is empty: completed 0, throughput 0.0, error_pct null, goodput 0.0. Window 2000 has all three: throughput 3 / 2 s = 1.5, error_pct 33.33 (the status 0), goodput 0.0 because the two successes waited 400 ms and 490 ms, both above 300 ms.

tests.name: Three 1 s windows with a 503, a timeout and a slow success; steady excludes the first second
Unsorted records; a record ending exactly at 1000 or 2000 ms counts in the window starting there
Windows with no completions report 0 throughput and a null error_pct
Every request fails (timeouts, 500 and 502): error_pct 100 and goodput 0
Goodput uses latency from intended_ms: late sends with fast service miss the SLO
Larger unsorted run: steady state 10-40 s excludes the ramp-up and ramp-down
No records: windows is empty, steady completed is 0 and error_pct is null
A steady interval whose end equals its start is rejected
